prompt: You change the basis in which an operator T is written. What changes?
options: Its rank, as the map is itself changed when the basis is
The map itself changes, since a different basis gives a different operator on the space
Its eigenvalues, as the basis fixes the values taken
Only its matrix representation; the map itself is unchanged
answer: Only its matrix representation; the map itself is unchanged
explanation: A basis change relabels coordinates. The underlying linear map, its eigenvalues and rank are intrinsic.
hint: Is the operator tied to the coordinates?

prompt: A linear map is one-to-one on an infinite-dimensional space. Is it automatically onto?
options: Yes, if it is continuous
No: a linear map on such a space cannot be one-to-one in general
Yes, as in finite dimensions
No: the right-shift on sequences is one-to-one but not onto
answer: No: the right-shift on sequences is one-to-one but not onto
explanation: The rank–nullity argument needs finite dimension. The right shift (x₁, x₂, …) → (0, x₁, x₂, …) misses vectors with nonzero first entry.
hint: Try the shift operator on sequences.

prompt: What do the columns of a matrix of a linear map represent?
options: Random constants that depend on the choice of the basis vectors in the space
The input basis vectors, written in the coordinates of the input space
The images of the input basis vectors, written in output coordinates
A list of eigenvalues, listed in the order of the basis vectors of the space
answer: The images of the input basis vectors, written in output coordinates
explanation: Column j is T(e_j). Linearity then determines T on every vector.
hint: Apply the matrix to the j-th basis vector.

explanation: Both output coordinates can be chosen independently.

prompt: When is the similarity transformation S⁻¹AS the right way to relate two matrices?
answer: When the same operator on one space is written in two bases
options: When the same operator on one space is written in two bases
For two matrices of the same size, as S⁻¹AS relates the pair
For diagonal matrices, where S⁻¹AS is the same map
When mapping between different spaces
explanation: A map between different input and output spaces needs separate basis changes on each side.
hint: Does the map go from a space to itself?

prompt: For A=[[1,2],[0,1]], find the first component of A(3,4).
hint: Matrix rows dot the column vector.
explanation: The first component is the first row dotted with (3, 4): 1 × 3 + 2 × 4 = 11.

prompt: For A=diag(2,3) and B=diag(4,5), find the first diagonal entry of AB.
explanation: AB is diagonal with entries multiplied entrywise, so the first entry is 2 × 4 = 8.
